analysis.one_liner: Bans exports of US-produced crude oil and natural gas, with limited presidential exemptions.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it sat in the Senate Banking Committee until the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would reinstate a ban on exporting crude oil and natural gas produced in the United States — a ban Congress lifted in 2015. The idea is to keep American-produced energy at home, where it would increase domestic supply and, its backers argue, hold down prices for US consumers. The President could grant exemptions in cases he deems consistent with the national interest, and could also restrict exports of coal, petroleum products, and petrochemical feedstocks [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: US households and businesses that buy gasoline, heating fuel, and electricity, if keeping crude oil and natural gas inside the country lowers domestic prices. Refineries and domestic manufacturers that use oil and gas as inputs would also gain from a larger, cheaper domestic supply.
analysis.who_benefits_short: US consumers of gasoline and heating fuel

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires the President to issue a rule prohibiting the export of crude oil and natural gas produced in the United States, so domestic production stays in the domestic market [S3].
The CRS summary states the President must ban exportation of US-produced crude oil and natural gas, with an exemption available only in specified circumstances [S2].

The bill also lets the President restrict exports of coal, petroleum products, natural gas, and petrochemical feedstocks, and to account for the historical trading relationship with Canada and Mexico when applying the rules [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Crude oil and natural gas producers, and the exporters and terminal operators who sell US oil and gas to foreign buyers, would lose access to export markets and the higher prices those markets often pay. Trade partners that depend on US energy supplies could also bear costs if exemptions are narrow.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas producers and export companies

drawbacks.text: An export ban is a blunt tool: it is not guaranteed to lower consumer prices, and it could discourage domestic drilling, since producers facing a smaller market may produce less over time, which would offset some supply benefit.

The bill allows the President to waive the usual public notice-and-comment period before imposing the export ban if he determines the delay would impair timely action, which concentrates significant power in the executive without normal public review [S3].

Cutting off or restricting US oil and gas exports could invite trade disputes with other countries and strain allies, particularly European countries that have leaned on US energy supplies in recent years; the bill's exemption process leaves those judgments entirely to the President [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill aims squarely at a problem working people feel — energy prices — and the mechanism (more supply staying in the US market) plausibly pushes domestic prices down. But the costs are real: it would transfer billions in revenue from oil and gas producers to consumers, could reduce production incentives over time, risks friction with trade partners, and hands the executive broad discretion over who gets an exemption. Whether the consumer savings outweigh those costs depends heavily on how the President writes and applies the rule.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which never held a hearing or vote, and the bill died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Markey introduced the bill on May 18, 2023, joined by four cosponsors — three Democrats and one Independent [S1] [S4].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs; no further action was ever taken [S5].
The bill never advanced out of committee and received no floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas producers and exporters keep their export markets, since the ban never advanced. US consumers see no change in energy policy either way.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas exporters keep export markets

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to reinstate the crude oil and natural gas export ban.

for.name: Sens. Jeff Merkley, Bernie Sanders, Elizabeth Warren, and Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; it never attracted support beyond these five senators.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: US oil and gas export industry
against.role: Exporters of crude oil and liquefied natural gas
against.what_they_did: The export ban would reverse a core industry objective, and the industry has long opposed reinstating export restrictions; no industry actor needed to act publicly because the bill stalled in committee.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors were Democrats or the Independent Bernie Sanders; no Republican supported it, and the Democratic-controlled Banking Committee never moved it.

industries.industry: Crude oil and natural gas producers and exporters
industries.note: The bill would strip them of export markets, which often pay higher prices than US buyers do. Their interest in continued exports runs directly against the bill's goal of holding down domestic energy prices.

The bill lets the President restrict exports of coal, petroleum products, and petrochemical feedstocks, though it does not require it, leaving these industries exposed to executive discretion rather than an outright ban.
Households and energy-intensive manufacturers would benefit if more domestic oil and gas stays in the US market, increasing supply and putting downward pressure on prices.
